questions.text:
At a local cafe, 60% of customers order coffee and 40% order tea. Of those who order coffee, 30% also order food. Of those who order tea, 50% also order food.

Draw a tree diagram showing all possible outcomes and their probabilities. Use the tree diagram to calculate the probability that a randomly selected customer orders food.
questions.expectedAnswer: P(food) = P(coffee and food) + P(tea and food) = 0.6 × 0.3 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.18 + 0.20 = 0.38
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Draws tree diagram with correct branches (coffee 0.6/tea 0.4, then food/no food for each). Calculates P(food) = 0.38. Merit: All probabilities correctly labelled on tree with clear working. Excellence: Fully communicated solution with tree diagram.

questions.text: Given that a customer ordered food, what is the probability that they ordered coffee? Show your working clearly.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies the need for conditional probability. Merit: Correctly applies P(coffee|food) = P(coffee and food)/P(food) = 0.18/0.38 = 0.474 (or 9/19). Excellence: Shows clear reasoning with formula stated, all values identified from the tree.

questions.text:
A spinner game at a school fair costs $2 to play. The spinner has the following outcomes:
• 50% chance of winning nothing ($0)
• 30% chance of winning $1
• 15% chance of winning $5
• 5% chance of winning $20

Calculate the expected value of the net gain (winnings minus cost) for a single play of this game.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Sets up the expected value calculation correctly with at least 3 of 4 terms. Merit: Correctly calculates expected winnings = $2.05 and net gain = $0.05. Excellence: Correctly calculates and interprets — on average a player gains 5 cents per game, so the game is approximately fair but very slightly favours the player.

questions.text:
The school wants to make a profit of at least $50 from this game. They expect 200 people to play.

By how much should they increase the cost per play so that their expected profit is at least $50? Show your working.
questions.expectedAnswer: Currently expected profit per play = -$0.05 (school loses 5c per player). For 200 plays, need profit ≥ $50, so profit per play ≥ $50/200 = $0.25. Current loss per play = $0.05. Need to increase cost by $0.05 + $0.25 = $0.30. New cost = $2.30.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Recognises that the school currently loses money per game and attempts to find the required increase. Merit: Correctly calculates that the cost needs to increase by $0.30 (to $2.30) so expected profit per play = $0.25, giving $50 over 200 plays. Excellence: Full solution with clear working and verification.

questions.text:
A two-way table shows survey results from 150 adults about exercise frequency and sleep quality.

|                    | Good sleep | Poor sleep | Total |
|--------------------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| Regular exercise   | 54        | 18        | 72    |
| Irregular exercise | 30        | 48        | 78    |
| Total              | 84        | 66        | 150   |

Calculate the probability that a randomly selected person has good sleep, given that they exercise regularly.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correctly identifies the conditional probability and calculates 54/72 = 0.75 (or 3/4).

questions.text:
A fitness company claims: 'Regular exercise causes better sleep — our data proves it since 75% of regular exercisers have good sleep compared to only 38% of irregular exercisers.'

Evaluate this claim. In your answer, discuss:
• the validity of the comparison
• whether the data supports a causal claim
• what other factors might explain the difference.
questions.expectedAnswer: The comparison is valid — there is a clear difference (75% vs 38.5%). However, the claim of causation is not justified from this observational survey data. Correlation does not imply causation. Confounding variables could explain the difference: people who exercise regularly may also have healthier diets, less stress, better routines, or different ages/occupations. A randomised controlled experiment would be needed to establish causation.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Notes there is a difference in proportions between the two groups. Merit: Correctly identifies that this is observational data so causation cannot be concluded, and suggests at least one confounding variable. Excellence: Thoroughly discusses the limitation of observational studies, provides multiple plausible confounding variables in context, and explains what type of study design would be needed to establish causation.
